== Certification systems ==
{{Main|Certified wood}}

[[Certified wood|Forest certification]] is a globally recognized system for encouraging sustainable forest management and assuring that forest-based goods are derived from sustainably managed forests.<ref name=":107"/><ref name=":110">{{Cite web |title=What is certification? |url=https://pefc.org/what-we-do/our-approach/what-is-certification |access-date=2023-01-30 |website=pefc.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=An Introduction to Forest Certification {{!}} NC State Extension Publications |url=https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/an-introduction-to-forest-certification |access-date=2023-01-30 |website=content.ces.ncsu.edu |language=en-US |archive-date=2023-01-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230129115609/https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/an-introduction-to-forest-certification |url-status=dead }}</ref> This is a voluntary procedure in which an impartial third-party organization evaluates the quality of forest management and output against a set of criteria established by a governmental or commercial certification agency.<ref name=":107"/><ref name=":110"/>

Growing [[environmental awareness]] and [[consumer demand]] for more socially responsible businesses helped third-party forest [[certification]] emerge in the 1990s as a credible tool for communicating the environmental and social performance of forest operations.

There are many potential users of certification, including: forest managers, scientists, policy makers, investors, environmental advocates, business consumers of wood and paper, and individuals.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

With third-party [[Certified wood|forest certification]], an independent [[Standards organization|standards setting organization (SSO)]] develops [[technical standard|standards]] of good forest management, and independent auditors issue certificates to forest operations that comply with those [[technical standard|standards]]. Forest certification verifies that forests are well-managed – as defined by a particular [[technical standard|standard]] – and chain-of-custody certification tracks wood and paper products from the certified forest through processing to the point of sale.{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

This rise of certification led to the emergence of several different systems throughout the world. As a result, there is no single accepted forest management [[international standard]] worldwide. [[ISO]] members<ref>{{cite web |date=20 October 2022 |title=Members |url=https://www.iso.org/members.html |website=so.org |publisher=International Organization for Standardization}}</ref> rejected a proposal for a forestry management system as requirements standard, with a consensus that a management system for certification would not be effective. Instead ISO members voted for a chain of custody of wood and wood-based products with ISO 38200 published in 2018. Without an [[international standard]] each system takes a somewhat different approach with scheme owners defining [[technical standard|private standards]] for sustainable forest management.

In its 2009–2010 Forest Products Annual Market Review United Nations Economic Commission for Europe/Food and Agriculture Organization stated: "Over the years, many of the issues that previously divided the (certification) systems have become much less distinct. The largest certification systems now generally have the same structural programmatic requirements."<ref>{{cite web |title=2009–2010 Forest Products Annual Market Review Page 121 |url=http://timber.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/publications/sp-25.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100820151542/http://timber.unece.org/fileadmin/DAM/publications/sp-25.pdf |archive-date=20 August 2010 |access-date=30 November 2011}}</ref>

Third-party forest certification is an important tool for those seeking to ensure that the paper and wood products they purchase and use come from forests that are well-managed and legally harvested. Incorporating third-party certification into forest product procurement practices can be a centerpiece for comprehensive wood and paper policies that include factors such as the protection of sensitive forest values, thoughtful material selection and efficient use of products.<ref>{{cite web |author=Erin Malec |date=5 October 2011 |title=Forest Certification Resource Center |url=http://www.metafore.org/?s=147 |access-date=30 November 2011 |publisher=Metafore.org |archive-date=22 January 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110122190944/http://www.metafore.org/?s=147 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
[[File:Forest Stewardship Council Logo.svg|thumb|203x203px|The [[Forest Stewardship Council]] is one of many [[forest certification]] programs.]]
Without a single [[international standard]], there are a proliferation of [[technical standard|private standards]],<ref>{{cite book |url=https://docplayer.net/23885374-International-standards-and-private-standards.html |title=International standards and private standards |date=2010 |publisher=International Organization for Standardization |isbn=978-92-67-10518-5}}</ref> with more than fifty scheme owners offering certification worldwide, addressing the diversity of forest types and tenures. Globally, the two largest umbrella certification programs are:
* [[Programme for the Endorsement of Forest Certification]] (PEFC)
* [[Forest Stewardship Council]] (FSC)
The Forest Stewardship Council's Policy on Conversion states that land areas converted from natural forests to round [[wood production]] after November 1994 are ineligible for Forest Stewardship Council certification.<ref name=":107" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=FSC Policy on Conversion |url=https://fsc.org/sites/default/files/2020-03/FSC-POL-01-007%20Policy%20on%20Conversion%20V1-0%20D1-0_EN.pdf |website=FSC}}</ref>

The area of forest certified worldwide is growing slowly. PEFC is the world's largest forest certification system, with more than two-thirds of the total global certified area certified to its Sustainability Benchmarks.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sorry, We didn't find what you were looking for | UNECE |url=https://unece.org/page404/timber%20docs%20fpama%202008%20FPAMR2008%20pdf |access-date=3 March 2024 |website=unece.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=PEFC |url=http://www.pefc.org/about-pefc/who-we-are/facts-a-figures |access-date=30 November 2011 |publisher=PEFC}}</ref> In 2021, PEFC issued a position statement<ref>{{cite web |date=11 March 2021 |title=PEFC response to the Greenpeace report, "Destruction: Certified" |url=https://pefc.org/news/pefc-response-to-greenpeace-report-destruction-certified |website=pefc.org |publisher=PEFC}}</ref> defending their use of [[technical standard|private standards]] in response to the Destruction: Certified report from [[Greenpeace]].<ref>{{cite web |date=10 March 2021 |title=Destruction: Certified |url=https://www.greenpeace.org/international/publication/46812/destruction-certified/ |website=greenpeace.org |publisher=Greenpeace International}}</ref>

In North America, there are three certification standards endorsed by PEFC – the Sustainable Forestry Initiative,<ref>{{cite web |title=Sustainable Forest Initiative |url=http://www.sfiprogram.org |access-date=30 November 2011 |publisher=Sfiprogram.org}}</ref> the Canadian Standards Association's Sustainable Forest Management Standard,<ref name=":4" /> and the American Tree Farm System.<ref>{{cite web |date=22 November 2011 |title=American Tree Farm System |url=http://www.treefarmsystem.org/ |access-date=30 November 2011 |publisher=Treefarmsystem.org}}</ref> SFI is the world's largest single forest certification standard by area.<ref>"SFI Inc. Launches New Standard, Leads Forest Certification Forward" (PDF). Archived from the original (PDF) on 2012-10-18. Retrieved 2013-02-19</ref> FSC has five standards in North America – one in the United States<ref>{{cite web |title=Forest Stewardship Council (US) |url=http://www.fscus.org/ |access-date=30 November 2011 |publisher=Fscus.org}}</ref> and four in Canada.<ref>{{cite web |title=Forest Stewardship Council (Canada) |url=http://www.fsccanada.org |access-date=30 November 2011 |publisher=Fsccanada.org}}</ref>

While certification is intended as a tool to enhance forest management practices throughout the world, to date most certified forestry operations are located in Europe and North America. A significant barrier for many forest managers in [[developing countries]] is that they lack the capacity to undergo a certification audit and maintain operations to a certification standard.<ref>Auer, M. (2012). 'Group forest certification for smallholders in Vietnam: An early test and future prospects'. ''Human ecology'' 40(1): 5–14.</ref>

== Forest governance ==
[[File:Richea_pandanifolia.jpg|thumb|Pandani ([[Richea pandanifolia]]) near Lake Dobson, [[Mount Field National Park]], Tasmania, Australia]]
[[File:Proportion of publicly owned forest area, by holder of management rights and region, 2020.svg|thumb|Proportion of publicly owned forest area, by holder of management rights and region, 2020.]]
Although a majority of forests continue to be owned formally by government, the effectiveness of forest governance is increasingly independent of formal ownership.<ref name="agrawal2008">Agrawal, A., Chhatre, A, and Hardin, R. (2008). 'Changing Governance of the World's Forest'. ''Science'' 320: 1460–1462</ref> Since neo-liberal ideology in the 1980s and the emanation of the [[climate change]] challenges, evidence that the state is failing to effectively manage environmental resources has emerged.<ref>Lutz, E, and Caldecott, J. (1996). Decentralization and biodiversity: a world bank symposium. Washington: The World Bank.</ref> Under [[neo-liberal]] regimes in the developing countries, the role of the state has diminished and the [[market forces]] have increasingly taken over the dominant socio-economic role.<ref>Hague, M. (1999). 'The Fate of sustainable development under neo-liberal regime in developing countries', ''International political review'' 20(2): 197–218.</ref>

The shifting of natural resource management responsibilities from central to state and local governments, where this is occurring, is usually a part of broader decentralization process.<ref>Margulis, S. {{date?}}. 'Decentralized environmental management', Annual World Bank Report.</ref>

The development of National Forest Funds is one way to address the issue of financing sustainable forest management.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://www.un.org/esa/forests/pdf/AGF_Study_July_2012.pdf |title=2012 STUDY ON FOREST FINANCING |date=June 2012 |publisher=Advisory Group on Finance Collaborative Partnership on Forests}}</ref> National forest funds (NFFs) are dedicated financing mechanisms managed by public institutions designed to support the conservation and sustainable use of forest resources.<ref name="auto">{{cite book |last1=Matta |first1=Rao |url=http://www.fao.org/3/a-i4359e.pdf |title=Towards effective national forest funds, FAO Forestry Paper 174 |publisher=Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations |year=2015 |isbn=978-92-5-108706-0 |location=Rome, Italy}}</ref> As of 2014, there are 70 NFFs operating globally.<ref name="auto" />

=== Community forestry ===
Community-based forest management (CBFM) is a scheme that links governmental forest agencies and the local community in efforts to regenerate degraded forests, reforest deforested areas, and decrease carbon emissions that contribute to climate change. This partnership is done with the intent of not only repairing damage to the environment but also providing economic and social benefits to the affected area.<ref name=":06">{{Cite journal |last=Singh |first=P |date=August 2008 |title=Exploring biodiversity and climate change benefits of community-based forest management |journal=Global Environmental Change |language=en |volume=18 |issue=3 |pages=468–478 |bibcode=2008GEC....18..468S |doi=10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2008.04.006}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mahanty |first1=Sango |last2=Gronow |first2=Jane |last3=Nurse |first3=Mike |last4=Malla |first4=Yam |date=2009-06-24 |title=Reducing Poverty through Community Based Forest Management in Asia |url=https://www.nepjol.info/index.php/JFL/article/view/1983 |journal=Journal of Forest and Livelihood |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=78–89 |doi=10.3126/jfl.v5i1.1983 |issn=1684-0186 |hdl-access=free |hdl=10535/8464}}</ref>

In principle, the benefits for the local community involvement in the management and protection of their forests would be to provide employment and to supplement income from both the wage labor and additional agriculture which would then strength the entire local economy while improving environmental conditions and mitigating climate change. Therefore, implementing a CBFM system can provide rural development while mitigating climate change and sustaining biodiversity within the region. It is important to engage the local community members, many of which are indigenous since presumably, they would have a deeper knowledge of the local ecosystems as well as the life cycles of those ecosystems over time. Their involvement also helps to ensure that their cultural practices remain intact.<ref name=":06" />

=== Proforestation ===
Proforestation is the practice of protecting existing natural [[forests]] to foster continuous growth, carbon accumulation, and structural complexity.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite journal |doi=10.3389/ffgc.2019.00027 |title=Intact Forests in the United States: Proforestation Mitigates Climate Change and Serves the Greatest Good |journal=Frontiers in Forests and Global Change|volume=2|year=2019|last1=Moomaw|first1=William R. |last2=Masino|first2=Susan A. |last3=Faison|first3=Edward K.|article-number=27 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2019FrFGC...2...27M }}</ref><ref name="10 rules">{{cite journal |last1=Di Sacco |first1=Alice |last2=Hardwick |first2=Kate A. |last3=Blakesley |first3=David |last4=Brancalion |first4=Pedro H. S. |last5=Breman |first5=Elinor |last6=Cecilio Rebola |first6=Loic |last7=Chomba |first7=Susan |last8=Dixon |first8=Kingsley |last9=Elliott |first9=Stephen |last10=Ruyonga |first10=Godfrey |last11=Shaw |first11=Kirsty |last12=Smith |first12=Paul |last13=Smith |first13=Rhian J. |last14=Antonelli |first14=Alexandre |title=Ten golden rules for reforestation to optimize carbon sequestration, biodiversity recovery and livelihood benefits |journal=Global Change Biology |date=25 January 2021 |volume=27 |issue=7 |pages=1328–1348 |doi=10.1111/gcb.15498 |pmid=33494123 |s2cid=225324365 |issn=1354-1013|doi-access=free |bibcode=2021GCBio..27.1328D |hdl=20.500.11937/88524 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> It is recognized as an important forest based strategy for addressing the global crises in [[climate]] and [[biodiversity]].<ref name="10 rules" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mackey |first1=Brendan |last2=Kormos |first2=Cyril F. |last3=Keith |first3=Heather |last4=Moomaw |first4=William R. |last5=Houghton |first5=Richard A. |last6=Mittermeier |first6=Russell A. |last7=Hole |first7=David |last8=Hugh |first8=Sonia |title=Understanding the importance of primary tropical forest protection as a mitigation strategy |journal=Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies for Global Change |date=1 May 2020 |volume=25 |issue=5 |pages=763–787 |doi=10.1007/s11027-019-09891-4 |s2cid=212681305 |language=en |issn=1573-1596|doi-access=free |bibcode=2020MASGC..25..763M |hdl=10072/394944 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> [[Forest restoration]] can be a strategy for [[climate change mitigation]].<ref name="AR6 WGIII Ch 13">IPCC (2022) [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_WGIII_SPM.pdf Summary for policy makers] in [https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg3/ Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change. Contribution of Working Group III to the Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change], Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, USA</ref>{{rp|37}} Proforestation complements other forest-based solutions like [[afforestation]], [[reforestation]] and improved forest management.

Allowing proforestation in some secondary forests will increase their accumulated carbon and biodiversity over time. Strategies for proforestation include [[Rewilding (conservation biology)|rewilding]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Protecting 50% of our Lands and Oceans |url=https://www.oneearth.org/protecting-50-of-our-lands-and-oceans/ |website=One Earth|date=23 May 2024 }}</ref> such as reintroducing [[apex predator]]s and [[keystone species]] as, for example, predators keep the population of herbivores in check (which reduce the [[Biosequestration|biomass of vegetation]]). Another strategy is establishing [[wildlife corridor]]s connecting isolated protected areas.<ref name="ReferenceA2">{{Cite web |date=3 April 2019 |title=The natural world can help save us from climate catastrophe | George Monbiot |url=http://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2019/apr/03/natural-world-climate-catastrophe-rewilding |website=The Guardian}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wilmers |first1=Christopher C. |last2=Schmitz |first2=Oswald J. |date=October 19, 2016 |title=Effects of gray wolf-induced trophic cascades on ecosystem carbon cycling |journal=Ecosphere |volume=7 |issue=10 |article-number=e01501 |doi=10.1002/ecs2.1501|doi-access=free |bibcode=2016Ecosp...7E1501W }}</ref>

Proforestation refers specifically to enabling continuous forest growth uninterrupted by active management or timber harvesting, a term coined by scientists [[William Moomaw]], Susan Masino, and Edward Faison.<ref name="e360.yale.edu">Fen Montaigne, [https://e360.yale.edu/features/why-keeping-mature-forests-intact-is-key-to-the-climate-fight Why Keeping Mature Forests Intact Is Key to the Climate Fight], ''Yale Environment 360'', 15 October 2019.</ref><ref name="ReferenceA" />

Proforestation differs from [[agroforestry]] or the cultivation of forest [[plantations]], the latter consisting of similarly aged trees of just one or two species. Plantations can be an efficient source of wood but often come at the expense of natural forests and cultivate little habitat for biodiversity, such as dead and fallen trees or understory plants. Further, once factoring in emissions from clearing the land and the decay of plantation waste and products at the end of their often brief lifecycles (e.g. paper products), plantations sequester 40 times less carbon than natural forests.<ref name="nature.com">{{cite journal |last1=Lewis |first1=Simon |last2=Wheeler |first2=Charlotte |last3=Mitchard |first3=Edward |last4=Koch |first4=Alexander |title=Restoring natural forests is the best way to remove atmospheric carbon |journal=Nature |date=4 April 2019 |volume=568 |issue=7750 |pages=25–28 |doi=10.1038/d41586-019-01026-8 |pmid=30940972 |s2cid=91190309 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019Natur.568...25L }}</ref>

Proforestation is specifically recommended in "World Scientists' Warning of a Climate Emergency, as a means to "quickly curtail [[habitat loss|habitat]] and [[biodiversity loss]]" and protect "high carbon stores" and areas "with the capacity to rapidly sequester carbon."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ripple |first1=William |last2=Wolf |first2=Christopher |last3=Newsome |first3=Thomas |last4=Barnard |first4=Phoebe |last5=Moomaw |first5=William |title=World Scientists' Warning of a Climate Emergency |journal=BioScience |date=January 2020 |volume=70 |issue=1 |pages=8–12 |doi=10.1093/biosci/biz088 |url=https://academic.oup.com/bioscience/article/70/1/8/5610806 |access-date=12 November 2020|doi-access=free |hdl=2445/151800 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==== Increasing Forest and Community Resilience ====
1.6 billion people worldwide depend on forests for their livelihoods, including 300–350 million (half of whom are Indigenous peoples) who live near or within "dense forests" and depend almost entirely on these ecosystems for their survival.<ref name="auto3">{{cite book |last1=Jenkins |first1=Michael |last2=Schaap |first2=Brian |title=Background Analytical Study 1: Forest Ecosystem Services |date=April 2018 |publisher=United Nations Forum on Forests |url=https://www.un.org/esa/forests/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/UNFF13_BkgdStudy_ForestsEcoServices.pdf |access-date=21 April 2021}}</ref> Rural households in Asia, Africa, and Latin America also depend on forests for about a quarter of their total incomes, with about half of this in the form of food, fodder, energy, building materials and medicine.<ref name="auto3"/>  
Proforestation can protect full native biodiversity and support the forests and other land types that provide resources we need. For example, research has found that old growth and complex forests are more resistant to the effects of climate change. One study found that taller trees had increased drought resistance, being able to capture and retain water better, due to their deeper root system and larger biomass. This means that even in dry conditions, these trees continued to photosynthesize at a higher rate than smaller trees.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Giardina |first1=Francesco |last2=et |first2=al |title=Tall Amazonian forests are less sensitive to precipitation variability |journal=Nature Geoscience |date=28 May 2018 |volume=11 |issue=6 |pages=405–409 |doi=10.1038/s41561-018-0133-5 |bibcode=2018NatGe..11..405G |s2cid=47004415 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-018-0133-5 |access-date=21 April 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref>   
Further, old-growth forests have been shown to be more resistant to fires compared to young forests with trees that have thinner bark and with more fuel available for increasing temperatures and fire damage.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Binkley |first1=Daniel |last2=Sisk |first2=Tom |last3=Chambers |first3=Carol |last4=Springer |first4=Judy |last5=Block |first5=William |title=The Role of Old-growth Forests in Frequent-fire Landscapes |journal=Ecology and Society |date=2007 |volume=12 |issue=2 |page=18 |doi=10.5751/ES-02170-120218 |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/rm/pubs_other/rmrs_2007_binkley_d001.pdf|doi-access=free }}</ref> Proforestation can help to reduce fire risks to forests and the surrounding communities. They can also help absorb water and prevent flooding to surrounding communities.<ref name="auto3"/> Considering the variety of ecosystem services complex forests provide, sustaining healthy forests means adjacent communities will be better off as well.

==History==
The [[Pre-industrial society|preindustrial age]] has been dubbed by [[Werner Sombart]] and others as the 'wooden age', as timber and firewood were the basic resources for energy, construction and housing. The development of modern forestry is closely connected with the rise of [[capitalism]], the economy as a science and varying notions of land use and property.<ref>compare Joachim Radkau Wood: A History, 2011</ref> Roman [[Latifundium|Latifundiae]], large agricultural estates, were quite successful in maintaining the large supply of wood that was necessary for the Roman Empire.<ref name="yale">The Nature of Mediterranean Europe: An Ecological History, by [[Alfred Thomas Grove]], [[Oliver Rackham]], Yale University Press, 2003, [http://yalepress.yale.edu/book.asp?isbn=9780300100556 review at Yale university press] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006140735/http://yalepress.yale.edu/book.asp?isbn=9780300100556|date=2014-10-06}} [https://muse.jhu.edu/login?auth=0&type=summary&url=/journals/journal_of_interdisciplinary_history/v032/32.3fagan.pdfThe Nature of Mediterranean Europe: An Ecological History (review) ][[Brian M. Fagan]]<span>, Journal of Interdisciplinary History, Volume 32, Number 3, Winter 2002, pp. 454-455 |</span> {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006073018/https://muse.jhu.edu/login?auth=0&type=summary&url=%2Fjournals%2Fjournal_of_interdisciplinary_history%2Fv032%2F32.3fagan.pdfThe|date=2014-10-06}}</ref> Large [[deforestation]]s came with the decline of the Romans.<ref name="yale" /> However  already in the 5th century, [[monk]]s in the then Byzantine [[Romagna]] on the [[Adriatic]] coast, were able to establish [[stone pine]] plantations to provide [[Firewood|fuelwood]] and [[Pine nut|food]].<ref name="Pines">{{cite book |last1=T. Mirov |first1=Nicholas |title=The story of pines |last2=Hasbrouck |first2=Jean |publisher=Indiana University Press |year=1976 |isbn=978-0-253-35462-4 |location=Bloomington and London |page=[https://archive.org/details/storyofpines00ntmi/page/111 111] |chapter=6 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/storyofpines00ntmi/page/111 |chapter-url-access=registration}}</ref> This was the beginning of the massive forest mentioned by [[Dante Alighieri]] in his 1308 poem [[Divine Comedy]].<ref name="Pines" />

Similar sustainable formal forestry practices were developed by the [[Visigoths]] in the 7th century when, faced with the ever-increasing shortage of wood, they instituted a code concerned with the preservation of [[oak]] and [[pine]] forests.<ref name="Pines" /> The use and management of many forest resources has a long history in China as well, dating back to the [[Han dynasty]] and taking place under the landowning [[gentry]]. A similar approach was used in Japan. It was also later written about by the [[Ming dynasty]] Chinese scholar [[Xu Guangqi]] (1562–1633).

In Europe, land usage rights in medieval and early modern times allowed different users to access forests and pastures. [[Plant litter]] and [[resin extraction]] were important, as [[pitch (resin)]] was essential for the [[caulking]] of ships, falking and hunting rights, firewood and building, timber gathering in [[wood pastures]], and grazing animals in forests. The notion of "[[commons]]" (German "Allmende") refers to the underlying traditional legal term of [[common land]]. The idea of enclosed private property came about during modern times. However, most hunting rights were retained by members of the nobility which preserved the right of the nobility to access and use common land for recreation, like [[fox hunting]].

=== 13th to 16th century ===
[[File:Forstarbeiten_in_Österreich.JPG|thumb|Forestry work in Austria]]
[[File:Gewinnung_von_Schnittreisig.jpg|thumb|Exploitation of brushwood at the [[:de:Goldner Steinrück|Golden Steinrueck]], [[Vogelsberg Mountains|Vogelsberg]]]]
[[File:Hans_Carl_von_Carlowitz.jpg|thumb|[[Hans Carl von Carlowitz]], German miner]]
Systematic management of forests for a [[sustainable yield]] of timber began in [[Portugal]] in the 13th century when [[Afonso III of Portugal|King Afonso III]] planted the Pinhal do Rei (King's Pine Forest) near [[Leiria]] to prevent coastal erosion and [[soil degradation]], and as a sustainable source for timber used in naval construction.<ref name="Livermore2004">{{cite book |author=H. V. Livermore |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7Cd0bKhByz8C&pg=PA15 |title=Portugal: A Traveller's History |publisher=Boydell Press |year=2004 |isbn=978-1-84383-063-4 |page=15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171211144023/https://books.google.com/books?id=7Cd0bKhByz8C&pg=PA15&lpg=PA15 |archive-date=2017-12-11 |url-status=live}}</ref> His successor [[Denis, King of Portugal|King Denis of Portugal]] continued the practice and the forest exists still today.<ref>{{cite web |title=PGF - Mata Nacional de Leiria — ICNF |url=http://www.icnf.pt/portal/florestas/gf/pgf/publicitacoes/drf-centro/2011/pgf-mn-leiria |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191210135748/http://www2.icnf.pt/portal/florestas/gf/pgf/publicitacoes/encerradas/dcnf-centr/pgf-mn-leiria |archive-date=2019-12-10 |access-date=2017-10-17 |website=www.icnf.pt}}</ref>

Forest management also flourished in the [[History of the forest in Central Europe|German]] states in the 14th century, e.g. in [[Nuremberg]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Buttinger |first=Sabine |year=2013 |title=Idee der Nachhaltigkeit |trans-title=The Idea of Sustainability |journal=[[Damals]] |language=de |volume=45 |issue=4 |page=8}}</ref> and in 16th-century [[Japan]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Forestry in Yashino |url=http://www.pref.nara.jp/nara/kaido/eg/syugen/d5_trad/trad1.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110628224026/http://www.pref.nara.jp/nara/kaido/eg/syugen/d5_trad/trad1.htm |archive-date=2011-06-28 |access-date=2010-10-12 |publisher=City of [[Nara, Nara]]}}</ref> Typically, a forest was divided into specific sections and mapped; the harvest of timber was planned with an eye to regeneration. As [[timber rafting]] allowed for connecting large continental forests, as in south western Germany, via Main, Neckar, Danube and Rhine with the coastal cities and states, early modern forestry and remote trading were closely connected. Large firs in the black forest were called "Holländer", as they were [[Timber trade|traded]] to the Dutch ship yards. Large timber rafts on the Rhine were 200 to 400m in length, 40m in width and consisted of several thousand logs. The crew consisted of 400 to 500 men, including shelter, bakeries, ovens and livestock stables.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dilibri.de/rlb/content/pageview/607408/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129034645/http://www.dilibri.de/rlb/content/pageview/607408/|title=Abbildungen der verschiedenen Gattungen von Fahrzeugen, wie man sie auf dem Rheine sieht / von H. Herman|date=October 3, 1820|archive-date=November 29, 2014|website=www.dilibri.de}}</ref> Timber rafting infrastructure allowed for large interconnected networks all over continental Europe and is still of importance in Finland.

Starting with the 16th century, enhanced world [[maritime trade]], a boom in housing construction in Europe, and the success and further [[Berggeschrey]] (rushes) of the mining industry increased timber consumption sharply. The notion of 'Nachhaltigkeit', [[sustainability]] in forestry, is closely connected to the work of [[Hans Carl von Carlowitz]] (1645–1714), a mining administrator in [[Saxony]]. His book ''Sylvicultura oeconomica, oder haußwirthliche Nachricht und Naturmäßige Anweisung zur wilden Baum-Zucht'' (1713) was the first comprehensive treatise about sustainable yield forestry.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dangel |first=Ulrich |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dP-xDQAAQBAJ&q=first+comprehensive+treatise+about+forestry&pg=PA30 |title=Turning Point in Timber Construction: A New Economy |date=2016-12-05 |publisher=Birkhäuser |isbn=978-3-0356-0863-2 |language=en}}</ref> In the UK, and, to an extent, in continental Europe, the [[enclosure]] movement and the [[Highland Clearances|Clearances]] favored  strictly enclosed private property.<ref name="Rad">Radkau, Joachim. Nature and Power. A Global History of the Environment. Cambridge University Press. 2008.</ref> The Agrarian reformers, early economic writers and scientists tried to get rid of the traditional commons.<ref name="rad1">Nature and Power, A Global History of the Environment, by Joachim Radkau, 2008, p. 72</ref> At the time, an alleged [[tragedy of the commons]] together with fears of a [[Holznot]], an imminent wood shortage played a watershed role in the controversies about cooperative land use patterns.<ref name="ws">The end of the commons as a watershed' ''The Age of Ecology'', Joachim Radkau, John Wiley & Sons, 03.04.2014,{{Clarify|reason=ambiguous date format|date=September 2017}} p. 15 ff</ref>

The practice of establishing tree plantations in the [[British Isles]] was promoted by [[John Evelyn]], though it had already acquired some popularity. [[Louis XIV of France|Louis XIV]]'s minister [[Jean-Baptiste Colbert]]'s oak [[Forest of Tronçais]], planted for the future use of the [[French Navy]], matured as expected in the mid-19th century: "Colbert had thought of everything except the steamship," [[Fernand Braudel]] observed.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Braudel |first=Fernand |title=The Wheels of Commerce: Civilization and Capitalism: 15th-18th Century (Volume II) |publisher=University of California Press |year=1979 |isbn=978-0-520-08115-4 |page=240}}</ref> Colbert's vision of forestry management was encoded in the [[French forestry ordinance of 1669|French forestry Ordinance of 1669]], which proved to be an influential management system throughout Europe.<ref>Kohler, Yann & Tissot, Wilfried. (2013). Integration of Nature Protection in Forest Policy in France - INTEGRATE Country Report.</ref> In parallel, schools of forestry were established beginning in the late 18th century in [[Hesse]], [[Russia]], [[Austria-Hungary]], [[Sweden]], [[France]] and elsewhere in Europe.

=== Mechanization in 19th century ===
Forestry mechanization was always in close connection to metal working and the development of mechanical tools to cut and transport timber to its destination.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Sundberg |first1=B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PiRffqqUcIQC&dq=Forestry+mechanization+was+always+in+close+connection+to+metal+working+and+the+development+of+mechanical+tools+to+cut+and+transport+timber+to+its+destination.&pg=PA1 |title=Operational Efficiency in Forestry: Vol. 1: Analysis |last2=Silversides |first2=C. R. |date=1988-04-30 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-90-247-3683-6 |language=en}}</ref> Rafting belongs to the earliest means of transport. Steel saws came up in the 15th century. The 19th century widely increased the availability of steel for [[whipsaw]]s and introduced [[forest railway]]s and railways in general for transport and as forestry customer. Further human induced changes, however, came since World War II, respectively in line with the "1950s syndrome".<ref>Christian Pfister (Hrsg.), Das 1950er Syndrom: Der Weg in die Konsumgesellschaft, Bern 1995</ref> The first portable chainsaw was invented in [[Chainsaw#History|1918 in Canada]], but large impact of mechanization in forestry started after World War II.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Silversides |first=C. R. |date=1984-08-01 |title=Mechanized Forestry, World War II to the Present |journal=The Forestry Chronicle |language=en |volume=60 |issue=4 |pages=231–235 |doi=10.5558/tfc60231-4 |issn=0015-7546 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Forestry [[Harvester (forestry)|harvesters]] are among the most recent developments. Although drones, [[Aerial Forest Protection Service (Russia)|planes]], [[Forest inventory#Tools used in inventory|laser scanning]], [[Landsat 5#Mission history|satellites]] and robots also play a part in forestry.

=== Forest conservation and early globalization ===
{{further|forest conservation}}

Starting from the 1750s modern [[scientific forestry]] was developed in France and the German speaking countries in the context of [[natural history]] scholarship and state administration inspired by [[physiocracy]] and [[cameralism]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Oosthoek |first1=K. Jan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6UItDwAAQBAJ&dq=Starting+from+the+1750s+modern+scientific+forestry+was+developed+in+France+and+the+German+speaking+countries+in+the+context+of+natural+history+scholarship+and+state+administration+inspired+by+physiocracy+and+cameralism.&pg=PA15 |title=Managing Northern Europe's Forests: Histories from the Age of Improvement to the Age of Ecology |last2=Hölzl |first2=Richard |date=2018-02-19 |publisher=Berghahn Books |isbn=978-1-78533-601-0 |language=en}}</ref> Its main traits were centralized management by professional foresters, the adherence to [[sustainable yield]] concepts with a bias towards fuelwood and timber production, artificial afforestation, and a critical view of pastoral and agricultural uses of forests.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hölzl |first=Richard |date=2010-12-01 |title=Historicizing Sustainability: German Scientific Forestry in the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries |journal=Science as Culture |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=431–460 |doi=10.1080/09505431.2010.519866 |issn=0950-5431 |s2cid=143441568}}</ref>

During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, forest preservation programs were established in [[British India]], the [[United States]], and Europe. Many foresters were either from continental Europe (like [[Dietrich Brandis|Sir Dietrich Brandis]]), or educated there (like [[Gifford Pinchot]]). Sir [[Dietrich Brandis]] is considered the father of tropical forestry, European concepts and practices had to be adapted in tropical and semi-arid climate zones. The development of [[plantation]] forestry was one of the (controversial) answers to the specific challenges in the tropical colonies. The enactment and evolution of [[Forestry law|forest laws]] and binding regulations occurred in most Western nations in the 20th century in response to growing conservation concerns and the increasing technological capacity of [[logging]] companies. [[Tropical forestry]] is a separate branch of forestry which deals mainly with equatorial forests that yield woods such as [[teak]] and [[mahogany]].

=== 21st century ===
A strong body of [[research]] exists regarding the management of [[Forest ecology|forest ecosystems]] and the genetic improvement of [[Tree breeding|tree species and varieties]]. Forestry studies also include the development of better methods for the planting, protecting, [[thinning]], [[controlled burn]]ing, [[felling]], extracting, and processing of [[timber]]. One of the applications of modern forestry is [[reforestation]], in which trees are planted and tended in a given area.<gallery mode="packed">
File:A_deciduous_beech_forest_in_Slovenia.jpg|A deciduous [[beech]] forest in [[Slovenia]]
File:Laser_guided_cutting_of_wood_inside_modern_woodmill.jpg|A modern [[sawmill]]
File:Employment_In_Agriculture,_Forestry_And_Fishing_By_Region.svg|A comparison of employment In agriculture, forestry and fishing by region
</gallery>Trees provide numerous environmental, social and economic benefits for people.<ref>{{cite web |title=Department of environmental conservation |url=http://www.dec.ny.gov/lands/4957.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150221114633/http://www.dec.ny.gov/lands/4957.html |archive-date=2015-02-21 |access-date=2014-11-29 |publisher=New York State Department}}</ref> In many regions, the [[forest industry]] is of major ecological, economic, and social importance, with the United States producing more [[timber]] than any other country in the world.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Casanova |first1=Vanessa |last2=Hamilton |first2=James |date=2019-04-03 |title=Non-Timber Forest Products in the Southeastern United States: Implications for Worker Safety and Health |journal=Journal of Agromedicine |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=121–124 |doi=10.1080/1059924X.2019.1578141 |issn=1059-924X |pmid=30712502 |s2cid=73422895}}</ref> Third-party [[certification]] systems that provide independent verification of sound forest [[stewardship]] and [[Sustainable forest management|sustainable forestry]] have become commonplace in many areas since the 1990s. These certification systems developed as a response to criticism of some forestry practices, particularly deforestation in less-developed regions along with concerns over resource management in the [[developed world]]. Sustainable forestry operations must also adhere to the [[International Labour Organization|International Labour Organization's]] 18 criteria on [[Human rights|human]] and social rights. [[Gender equality]], health and well-being and community consultation are examples of mentioned rights.<ref name="auto2"/><ref name=":107"/>

In topographically severe forested terrain, proper forestry is important for the prevention or minimization of serious soil [[erosion]] or even [[landslide]]s. In areas with a high potential for landslides, forests can [[Erosion control|stabilize soils]] and prevent property damage or loss, human injury, or loss of life.

Global production of roundwood rose from 3.5 billion m''³'' in 2000 to 4 billion m''³'' in 2021. In 2021, wood fuel was the main product with a 49 percent share of the total (2 billion m''³''), followed by coniferous industrial roundwood with 30 percent (1.2 billion m''³'') and non-coniferous industrial roundwood with 21 percent (0.9 billion m''³''). Asia and the Americas are the two main producing regions, accounting for 29 and 28 percent of the total roundwood production, respectively; Africa and Europe have similar shares of 20–21 percent, while Oceania produces the remaining 2 percent.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |url=http://www.fao.org/documents/card/en/c/cc8166en |title=World Food and Agriculture – Statistical Yearbook 2023 |date=2023-11-29 |publisher=FAO |isbn=978-92-5-138262-2 |language=en |doi=10.4060/cc8166en}}</ref>

Many lower- and middle-income countries rely on wood for energy purposes (notably cooking). The largest producers are all in these income groups and have large populations with a high reliance on wood for energy: in 2021, India ranked first with 300 million m''³'' (15 percent of total production), followed by China with 156 million m3 and Brazil with 129 million m''³'' (8 percent and 7 percent of global production).<ref name=":2" />

== Society and culture ==

=== Public input and awareness ===
[[Image:Amazonie deforestation.jpg|thumb|right|230px|[[Deforestation]] and increased road-building in the [[Amazon rainforest]] are a significant concern because of increased human encroachment upon wild areas, increased resource extraction and further threats to [[biodiversity]].]]
There has been increased public awareness of natural resource policy, including forest management.{{citation needed|date=May 2018}} Public concern regarding forest management may have shifted from the extraction of timber for economic development, to maintaining the flow of the range of ecosystem services provided by forests, including provision of habitat for [[wildlife]], protecting [[biodiversity]], [[Drainage basin|watershed]] management, and opportunities for [[recreation]]. Increased environmental awareness may contribute to an increased public mistrust of forest management professionals.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Shindler |first=Bruce |author2=Lori A. Cramer |date=January 1999 |title=Shifting Public Values for Forest Management: Making Sense of Wicked Problems |url=http://www.fs.fed.us/eco/eco-watch/wickedpr.html |journal=Western Journal of Applied Forestry |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=28–34 |doi=10.1093/wjaf/14.1.28 |issn=0885-6095 |access-date=2008-08-25 |doi-access=free}}</ref> But it can also lead to greater understanding about what professionals do for forests for nature conservation and ecological services.

== By region ==

=== Developing world ===
{{See also|Deforestation}}
In December 2007, at the Climate Change Conference in [[Bali]], the issue of [[deforestation]] in the developing world in particular was raised and discussed. The foundations of a new incentive mechanism for encouraging sustainable forest management measures was therefore laid in hopes of reducing world deforestation rates. This mechanism was formalized and adopted as REDD in November 2010 at the Climate Change Conference in Cancun by UNFCCC COP 16.  Developing countries who are signatories of the [[Convention on Biological Diversity|CBD]] were encouraged to take measure to implement REDD activities in the hope of becoming more active contributors of global efforts aimed at the mitigation greenhouse gas, as deforestation and forest degradation account for roughly 15% of total global greenhouse gas emissions.<ref>{{cite web |title=What is REDD+? |url=https://www.forestcarbonpartnership.org/what-redd |access-date=4 March 2020 |website=The Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF) |publisher=Forest Carbon Partnership Facility}}</ref> The REDD activities are formally tasked with "reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation; and the role of conservation, sustainable management of forests and enhancement of forest carbon stocks in developing countries".  REDD+ works in 3 phases. The first phase consists of developing viable strategies, while the second phase begins work on technology development and technology transfer to the developing countries taking part in REDD+ activities. The last phase measures and reports the implementation of the action taken.<ref>{{cite web |date=15 June 2012 |title=REDD+ and Biodiversity Benefits |url=https://www.cbd.int/forest/redd-plus/ |access-date=4 March 2020 |website=Convention on Biological Diversity |publisher=United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity}}</ref> In 2021 the LEAF coalition was created, aiming to provide 1 billion dollars to countries that will protect their tropical and subtropical forests.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Marchant |first1=Natalie |date=21 May 2021 |title=Can this billion-dollar initiative save the world's tropical forests? |url=https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2021/05/amazon-coalition-finance-tropical-forests-protection/ |access-date=28 May 2021 |website=World Economic Forum}}</ref>

=== European Union ===
In 2022 the [[European Parliament|European parliament]] approved a bill aiming to stop the import linked with deforestation. The bill may cause to Brazil, for example, to stop deforestation for agricultural production and begun to "increase productivity on existing agricultural land".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Schröder |first1=André |date=15 September 2022 |title=European bill passes to ban imports of deforestation-linked commodities |url=https://news.mongabay.com/2022/09/european-bill-passes-to-ban-imports-of-deforestation-linked-commodities/ |access-date=18 September 2022 |website=Mongabay}}</ref> The legislation was adopted with some changes by the [[European Council]] in May 2023 and is expected to enter into force several weeks after. The bill requires companies who want to import certain types of products to the European Union to prove the production of those commodities is not linked to areas deforested after 31 of December 2020. It prohibits also import of products linked with [[Human rights]] abuse. The list of products includes: [[palm oil]], [[cattle]], [[wood]], [[coffee]], [[Cocoa bean|cocoa]], [[rubber]] and [[Soybean|soy]]. Some derivatives of those products are also included: [[chocolate]], [[furniture]], [[Paper|printed paper]] and several palm oil based derivates.<ref>{{cite web |title=Council adopts new rules to cut deforestation worldwide |url=https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2023/05/16/council-adopts-new-rules-to-cut-deforestation-worldwide/ |access-date=22 May 2023 |website=European Counsil |publisher=European Union}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Téllez Chávez |first1=Luciana |date=16 May 2023 |title=EU Approves Law for 'Deforestation-Free' Trade |url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/05/16/eu-approves-law-deforestation-free-trade |access-date=22 May 2023 |website=Human Rights Watch}}</ref>

=== Great Britain ===
The [[Forestry Commission]] was founded in 1919 to restore forests to Great Britain after [[World War I|World War 1]]. The commission regulates both private and public forests, as well as manages private forests. Agricultural land was bought and transformed, totalling 35% of the British woodland area having been possessed at one point in time<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Aldhous |first1=J. |year=1997 |title=British forestry: 70 years of achievement |journal=Forestry |volume=70 |issue=4 |pages=283–292 |doi=10.1093/forestry/70.4.283 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== America ===

==== Canada ====
Canada's significant contribution to global sustainable forest management with its 166 million hectares of forest land independently certified as sustainably managed, representing 40% of the world's certified forests, which is more than any other country.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Service |first1=Canadian Forest |url=https://ostrnrcan-dostrncan.canada.ca/handle/1845/250554 |access-date=2024-04-10 |website=ostrnrcan-dostrncan.canada.ca | title=Sustainable Forest Management in Canada. Key Facts |date=2016 |publisher=Natural Resources Canada = Ressources naturelles Canada |isbn=978-0-660-04418-7 }}</ref> Approximately 94% of Canada's forest land is publicly owned. Sustainable forest management strategies aim to reconcile various immediate demands while ensuring that forests continue to provide benefits for future generations.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2022-06-03 |title=Sustainable forest management in Canada |url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/our-natural-resources/forests/sustainable-forest-management/sustainable-forest-management-canada/24361 |access-date=2024-04-12 |website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref>

The province of [[Ontario]] has its own sustainable forest management measures in place. A little less than half of all the publicly owned forests of [[Ontario]] are managed forests, required by The Crown Forest Sustainability Act to be managed sustainably. Sustainable management is often done by forest companies who are granted Sustainable Forest Licenses which are valid for 20 years. The main goal of Ontario's sustainable forest management measures is to ensure that the forest are kept healthy and productive, conserving biodiversity, all whilst supporting communities and forest industry jobs. All management strategies and plans are highly regulated, arranged to last for a 10-year period, and follow the strict guidelines of the Forest Management Planning Manual. Alongside public sustainable forest management, the government of Ontario encourages sustainable forest management of Ontario's private forests as well through incentives.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Sustainable forest management |url=https://www.ontario.ca/page/sustainable-forest-management |access-date=3 March 2020 |website=Ontario.ca |date=17 July 2014 |publisher=Government of Ontario}}</ref> So far, 44% of Ontario's crown forests are managed.<ref name=":0" />

In order for logging to begin, the forestry companies must present a plan to the government who will then communicate to the public, First Nations and other industries in order to protect forest values. The plan must include strategies on how the forest values will be protected, assessing the state of the forest and whether it is capable of recovering from human activity, and presenting strategies on regeneration.  After the harvest begins, the government monitors if the company is complying within the planned restrictions and also monitors the health of the ecosystem<ref name="Canada">{{Cite web |last=Canada |first=Natural Resources |date=2015-05-25 |title=Canada's forest laws |url=https://www.nrcan.gc.ca/our-natural-resources/forests/sustainable-forest-management/canadas-forest-laws/17497 |access-date=2022-03-31 |website=www.nrcan.gc.ca}}</ref> (soil depletion and erosion, water contamination, wildlife...). Failure to comply may result in fines, suspensions, removal of harvesting rights, confiscation of harvested timber and possible imprisonment.<ref name="Canada" />

==== United States ====
In the beginning of the year 2020 the "Save the Redwoods League" after a successful crowdfunding campaign bought " Alder Creek" a piece of land 583 acres large, with 483 big Sequoia trees including the 5th largest tree in the world. The organizations plan to make there forest thinning<ref>{{cite news |last1=Rosane |first1=Olivia |date=10 January 2020 |title=World's Fifth-Largest Tree Now Safe From Loggers in an 'Inspiring Outpouring of Generosity' |url=https://www.ecowatch.com/giant-sequoia-safe-from-loggers-2644664254.html |access-date=12 January 2020 |agency=Ecowatch}}</ref> that is a controversial operation<ref>{{cite web |title=Stop Thinning Forests |url=https://stopthinningforests.org/index.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200112090136/https://stopthinningforests.org/index.html |archive-date=12 January 2020 |access-date=12 January 2020 |website=Stop Thinning Forests}}</ref>{{excerpt|Forest conservation in the United States}}

=== Asia ===

==== Russia ====
In 2019 after severe wildfires and public pressure the Russian government decided to take a number of measures for more effective forest management, what is considered as a big victory for the [[Environmental movement]]<ref>{{cite news |last1=Vasilieva |first1=Tatiana |title=Life in the Siberian haze |url=https://www.greenpeace.org/international/story/23919/russian-wildfires-blog-siberian-haze/ |access-date=3 September 2019 |website=Greenpeace International}}</ref>

==== Indonesia ====
In August 2019, a court in Indonesia stopped the construction of a dam that could heavily hurt forests and villagers in the area<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hanafiah |first1=Junaidi |date=2 September 2019 |title=Indonesian court cancels dam project in last stronghold of tigers, rhinos |url=https://news.mongabay.com/2019/09/indonesian-court-cancels-dam-project-in-last-stronghold-of-tigers-rhinos/ |access-date=9 September 2019 |agency=Mongabay}}</ref>

In 2020 the rate of [[deforestation in Indonesia]] was the slowest since 1990. It was 75% lower than in 2019. This is because the government stopped issuing new licences to cut forests, including for palm oil plantations. The falling price of palm oil facilitated making it. Very wet weather reduced wildfires what also contributed to the achievement.<ref>{{cite web |title=Deforestation In Indonesia Has Hit A Record Low |url=https://www.weforum.org/videos/23212-deforestation-in-indonesia-has-hit-a-record-low |access-date=16 July 2021 |website=World Economic Forum}}</ref>

=== Africa ===

==== Congo ====
In August 2021 [[UNESCO]] removed the [[Salonga National Park]] from its list of threatened sites. Forbidding oil drilling, reducing poaching played crucial role in the  achievement. The event is considered as a big win to [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]] as the Salonga forest is the biggest protected rainforest in Africa.<ref>{{cite news |date=8 August 2021 |title=UNESCO Removes Salonga National Park From World Heritage 'Danger' List |url=https://voi.id/en/news/73533/unesco-hapus-taman-nasional-salonga-dari-daftar-bahaya-warisan-dunia |access-date=15 August 2021 |agency=VOI |archive-date=15 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210815080917/https://voi.id/en/news/73533/unesco-hapus-taman-nasional-salonga-dari-daftar-bahaya-warisan-dunia }}</ref>

==== Kenya ====
In accordance with Article 10 of the Kenyan Constitution, which mandates the incorporation of sustainable development into all laws and decisions regarding public policy, including forest conservation and management. Kenya responds to continued deforestation, forest degradation, and forest encroachment, which results in conversion of land uses to settlement and agriculture, by taking action.<ref>{{cite web |title=EMC Forest Management and Tree Growing Policy |url=https://info.undp.org/docs/pdc/Documents/KEN/EMC%20Forest%20Management%20and%20Tree%20Growing%20Policy.pdf |access-date=3 March 2024 |website=UNDP}}</ref>

This includes management for timber, [[aesthetics]], [[outdoor recreation|recreation]], urban values, [[watershed management|water]], [[wildlife]], inland and nearshore fisheries, [[forest product|wood products]], [[plant genetic resources]], and other [[Nontimber forest products|forest resource values]].<ref>{{cite web | title = Glossary of Forestry Terms in British Columbia | publisher = Ministry of Forests and Range (Canada) | date = March 2008| url = http://www.for.gov.bc.ca/hfd/library/documents/glossary/Glossary.pdf | access-date = 2009-04-06}}</ref> Management objectives can be for conservation, utilisation, or a mixture of the two. ==Role of forests==
{{Main|Forest}}

The forest is a natural system that can supply different products and services. Forests supply water, [[Climate change mitigation|mitigate climate change]], provide habitats for wildlife including many pollinators which are essential for sustainable food production, provide timber and fuelwood, serve as a source of non-wood forest products including food and medicine, and contribute to rural livelihoods.<ref name=":3"/> The working of a forest is influenced by the natural environment: climate, topography, soil, etc., and also by human activity. The actions of humans in forests constitute forest management.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Natural Forest Management |url=https://www.fao.org/forestry/sfm/85084/en/ |access-date=2022-10-24 |website=www.fao.org |archive-date=2022-12-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221226123935/https://www.fao.org/forestry/sfm/85084/en/ }}</ref>

== Aims ==
Some forests have been and are managed to obtain traditional forest products such as firewood, fiber for paper, and timber, with little thinking for other products and services. Nevertheless, as a result of the progression of environmental awareness, management of forests for multiple use is becoming more common.<ref name="Young">{{cite book |last1=Young |first1=Raymond |title=Introduction to Forest Science |date=1982 |publisher=John Wiley & sons |isbn=978-0-471-06438-1|page=207}}</ref>

Forests provide a variety of [[ecosystem service]]s: cleaning the air, accumulating carbon, filtering water, and reducing flooding and erosion.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ecosystem Services |url=https://research.fs.usda.gov/centers/ccrc |access-date=21 April 2021 |website=Climate Change Resource Center |publisher=USDA and US Forest Service}}</ref> Forests are the most biodiverse land-based ecosystem, and provide habitat for a vast array of animals, birds, plants and other life. They can provide food and material and also opportunities for recreation and education. Research has found that forest plantations "may result in reduced diversity and abundance of pollinators compared with natural forests that have greater structural and plant species diversity."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brockerhoff |first1=Eckehard |last2=et |first2=al |date=4 November 2017 |title=Forest biodiversity, ecosystem functioning and the provision of ecosystem services |journal=Biodiversity and Conservation |volume=26 |issue=13 |pages=3005–3035 |bibcode=2017BiCon..26.3005B |doi=10.1007/s10531-017-1453-2 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Coverage ==
Globally in 2025, 1.20 billion ha of forest (29% of the total forest area) is managed primarily to produce wood and non-wood forest products. In addition, about 616 million ha of forest is designated for multiple use, which often includes production. The largest forest area designated for production is in Europe, at 548 million ha, which is more than half the region’s total forest area and almost half the total forest area designated for production globally. The area of forest designated primarily for production and multiple use worldwide decreased by 29.8 million ha and 97.5 million ha, respectively, between 1990 and 2025.<ref name=":7" />

== Monitoring and planning ==
[[File:Proportion of total forest area designated for various primary management objectives, 2025.svg|thumb|Proportion of total forest area worldwide designated for various primary management objectives, 2025.]]
[[File:Proportion of forest area with long-term management plans, by region, 2025.svg|thumb|Proportion of forest area with long-term management plans, by region, 2025.]]
Foresters develop and implement forest management plans relying on mapped resources, [[Forest inventory|inventories]] showing an area's [[Topography|topographical]] features as well as its distribution of trees (by species) and other plant covers. Plans also include landowner objectives, roads, [[culvert]]s, proximity to human habitation, water features and hydrological conditions, and soil information. Forest management plans typically include recommended [[Silviculture|silvicultural]] treatments and a timetable for their implementation. Application of digital maps in Geographic Information systems (GIS) that extracts and integrates different information about forest terrains, [[soil type]] and tree covers, etc. using, e.g. laser scanning enhances forest management plans in modern systems.<ref>{{Cite web |last=eugene |date=2022-09-20 |title=What is Geographic Information System Analysis In Forestry? |url=https://tallpinesforestmanagement.com/2022/09/20/what-is-gis-analysis-and-whats-its-role-in-forest-management/ |access-date=2023-01-23 |website=Tall Pines Forest Management |language=en-US}}</ref>

Forest management plans include recommendations to achieve the landowner's objectives and desired future conditions for the property subject to ecological, financial, logistical (e.g. access to resources), and other constraints.  On some properties, plans focus on producing quality wood products for processing or sale. Hence, tree species, quantity, and form, all central to the value of harvested products quality and quantity, tend to be important components of silvicultural plans.

Good management plans include consideration of future conditions of the stand after any recommended harvests treatments, including future treatments (particularly in intermediate stand treatments), and plans for natural or artificial regeneration after final harvests.

The objectives of [[landowner]]s and [[Leasehold estate|leaseholders]] influence plans for harvest and subsequent site treatment. In Britain, plans featuring "good forestry practice" must always consider the needs of other stakeholders such as nearby communities or rural residents living within or adjacent to woodland areas. Foresters consider tree felling and environmental legislation when developing plans. Plans instruct the sustainable harvesting and replacement of trees.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Garcia-Grant |first=Ian |date=Dec 20, 2021 |title=Planning For Long Term Forest Management |url=https://tallpinesforestmanagement.com/2021/12/20/planning-for-long-term-forest-management/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221202232002/https://tallpinesforestmanagement.com/2021/12/20/planning-for-long-term-forest-management/ |archive-date=Dec 2, 2022 |access-date=Jan 23, 2023 |website=Tall Pines Forest Management}}</ref> They indicate whether road building or other forest engineering operations are required.

[[Agriculture]] and forest leaders are also trying to understand how the [[Politics of climate change|climate change legislation]] will affect what they do. The information gathered will provide the data that will determine the role of agriculture and forestry in a new climate change regulatory system.<ref name="galegroup1">{{cite web |url=http://find.galegroup.com/gps/start.do?prodId=IPS |title=PowerSearch Logout |publisher=Find.galegroup.com |access-date=2014-03-15 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130510172355/http://find.galegroup.com/gps/start.do?prodId=IPS |archive-date=2013-05-10 }}</ref>

=== Forest inventory ===

{{main|Forest inventory}}

Forest inventory is the systematic collection of data and forest information for assessment or analysis. An estimate of the value and possible uses of [[timber]] is an important part of the broader information required to [[sustainability|sustain ecosystems]].<ref name="Moores_et_al">{{Citation |journal=Environmental Monitoring and Assessment |year=1996 |volume=39 |issue=1–3 |pages=571–577 |title=Forest ecological classification and mapping: their application for ecosystem management in Newfoundland |author1=L. J. Moores |author2=B. Pittman |author3=G. Kitchen |doi=10.1007/bf00396169|pmid=24198030 |bibcode=1996EMnAs..39..571M |s2cid=206779166 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-06-14 |title=An Introduction To The Business Of Small-scale Forestry. Private Forestry Guidance Materials Report 2023 |url=https://fwpa.com.au/report/an-introduction-to-the-business-of-small-scale-forestry/ |access-date=2025-02-06 |website=FWPA}}</ref>

===Wildlife considerations===

The abundance and diversity of birds, mammals, amphibians and other wildlife are affected by strategies and types of forest management.<ref>*Philip Joseph Burton. 2003. ''Towards sustainable management of the boreal forest'' 1039 pages</ref> Forests are important because they provide these species with food, space and water.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Home {{!}} Ohio Woodland Stewards Program |url=https://woodlandstewards.osu.edu/ |access-date=2022-10-24 |website=woodlandstewards.osu.edu}}</ref> Forest management is also important as it helps in conservation and utilization of the forest resources.Forest clearing to aid specific species of wildlife has been criticized because it can fragment forests leading to deleterious effects.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kellett |first1=Michael J. |last2=Maloof |first2=Joan E. |last3=Masino |first3=Susan A. |last4=Frelich |first4=Lee E. |last5=Faison |first5=Edward K. |last6=Brosi |first6=Sunshine L. |last7=Foster |first7=David R. |date=2023-01-09 |title=Forest-clearing to create early-successional habitats: Questionable benefits, significant costs |journal=Frontiers in Forests and Global Change |language=English |volume=5 |article-number=1073677 |doi=10.3389/ffgc.2022.1073677 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2023FrFGC...573677K |issn=2624-893X}}</ref>{{citation needed|date=July 2023}}

Approximately 50 million hectares (or 24%) of European forest land is protected for biodiversity and landscape protection. Forests allocated for soil, water, and other ecosystem services encompass around 72 million hectares (32% of European forest area).<ref name=":107">{{Cite book |last=Bank |first=European Investment |url=https://www.eib.org/en/publications/20220173-forests-at-the-heart-of-sustainable-development |title=Forests at the heart of sustainable development: Investing in forests to meet biodiversity and climate goals |date=2022-12-08 |publisher=European Investment Bank |isbn=978-92-861-5403-4 |language=EN}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Forests - Environment - European Commission |url=https://ec.europa.eu/environment/forests/policy_en.htm |access-date=2023-01-30 |website=ec.europa.eu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://foresteurope.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/08/protected-forests-in-europe.pdf|title=Protected Forests in Europe}}</ref> Over 90% of the world's forests regenerate organically, and more than half are covered by forest management plans or equivalents.<ref name=":107"/><ref name=":6" />

===Management intensity===
[[File:Proportion of forest area with long-term management plans, by region, 2020.svg|thumb|Proportion of forest area with long-term management plans, by region, 2020<ref name="auto1">{{Cite book|title=Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020 – Key findings|publisher=FAO|year=2020|isbn=978-92-5-132581-0|location=Rome|doi=10.4060/ca8753en|s2cid=130116768 }}</ref>]]

Forest management varies in intensity from a leave alone, natural situation to a highly intensive regime with silvicultural interventions. Forest Management is generally increased in intensity to achieve either economic criteria (increased timber yields, [[non-timber forest product]]s, [[ecosystem services]]) or ecological criteria (species recovery, fostering of rare species, carbon sequestration).<ref>{{Cite journal | title=Classification of Forest Management Approaches: A New Conceptual Framework and Its Applicability to European Forestry | author1=Philipp S. Duncker | author2=Susana M. Barreiro | author3=Geerten M. Hengeveld | author4=Torgny Lind | author5=William L. Mason  | author6=Slawomir Ambrozy | author7=Heinrich Spiecker | url=http://www.ecologyandsociety.org/vol17/iss4/art51/ | journal=Ecology and Society | date=2012 | volume=17 | issue=4 | article-number=art51 | doi=10.5751/ES-05262-170451 }}</ref>

Most of the forests in Europe have management plans; on the other hand, management plans exist for less than 25 percent of forests in Africa and less than 20 percent in South America. The area of forest under management plans is increasing in all regions – globally, it has increased by 233 million ha since 2000, reaching 2.05 billion ha in 2020.<ref name="auto1"/>

=== Monitoring ===
Long-term monitoring studies are conducted to track forest dynamics over extended periods.<ref name="Prevedello Winck Weber et al 2019"/><ref name="Benedek & Fertő 2013"/> These studies involve monitoring factors such as tree growth, mortality rates, and species composition. By observing forest changes over time, scientists can assess the health of forests and their responses to environmental shifts. Long-term monitoring is invaluable for informing sustainable forest management practices.<ref name="Zhang & Wei 2021"/><ref name="Anderegg Wu Acil et al 2022"/> Yet such monitoring is usually of the type that provide "early warning" only, while a more valuable approach would be to combine long-term monitoring and long-term experiments, thereby revealing causality <ref>Nichols, J.D & Williams, B.K. (2006). Monitoring for conservation. Trends in Ecology 21: 668-673.</ref>     

Scientific research employs [[Remote sensing|remote sensing technologies]] and [[geographic information system]]s (GIS) to monitor changes in forest cover, deforestation rates, and forest health over time.<ref name="Zhang & Wei 2021"/><ref name="AbdulBaqi2022"/> These tools provide valuable data for forest assessments and support evidence-based decision making in forest management and conservation. By remotely monitoring forest changes, scientists can respond more effectively to threats and challenges facing forests.<ref name="Zhang & Wei 2021" /><ref name="AbdulBaqi2022" />

Researchers conduct [[biodiversity]] assessments to gain insights into the diversity and distribution of plant and animal species in various forest ecosystems.<ref name="Prevedello Winck Weber et al 2019"/><ref name="Zhang & Wei 2021"/> These studies are essential for identifying areas of high conservation value and understanding the ecological importance of different habitats. By studying biodiversity patterns, scientists can recommend targeted approaches to forest management that protect and promote the richness of forest life.<ref name="Windisch Davin Seneviratne 2021"/><ref name="Anderegg Wu Acil et al 2022"/><ref name="Prevedello Winck Weber et al 2019" /><ref name="Portmann Beyerle Davin et al 2022"/>

=== Effects of climate change on forests ===
{{Further|Effects of climate change on biomes}}
Research explores the specific [[Effects of climate change on biomes|impacts of climate change on forest ecosystems]], including extreme heat and drought events.<ref name="Prevedello Winck Weber et al 2019"/><ref name="Anderegg Wu Acil et al 2022"/> Understanding these effects is vital for developing [[Climate change adaptation|adaptive strategies]] to mitigate climate change impacts on forests. By recognizing the vulnerabilities of forests to changing climatic conditions, scientists can implement conservation methods that enhance their resilience.<ref name="Portmann Beyerle Davin et al 2022"/><ref name="Windisch Davin Seneviratne 2021"/><ref name="Anderegg Wu Acil et al 2022" />

Scientific research plays a crucial role in forest management by utilizing [[climate model]]ing to project future [[Climate change scenario|climate scenarios]].<ref name="Anderegg Wu Acil et al 2022"/><ref name="Benedek & Fertő 2013"/><ref name="Windisch Davin Seneviratne 2021"/> These models help scientists understand potential changes in temperature, precipitation patterns, and extreme weather events, enabling them to assess the impact of these changes on forest ecosystems. By predicting climate trends, researchers can develop more effective strategies for forest management and conservation.<ref name="Zhang & Wei 2021"/><ref name="Anderegg Wu Acil et al 2022" /><ref name="Windisch Davin Seneviratne 2021" />

== Methods for creating or recreating forests ==
The term ''forestation'' is sometimes used as an umbrella term to include [[afforestation]] and [[reforestation]]. Both of those are processes for establishing and nurturing [[forest]]s on lands that either previously had forest cover or were subjected to [[deforestation]] or degradation.<ref name="Prevedello Winck Weber et al 2019"/>

=== Hardwood timber production ===
Hardwood timber production is the process of managing stands of [[deciduous]] trees to maximize woody output. The production process is not linear because other factors must be considered, including marketable and non-marketable goods, financial benefits, management practices, and the environmental implications, of those management practices.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Nyland |first=Ralph D. |title=Silviculture: concepts and applications |date=2002 |publisher=McGraw-Hill |isbn=978-0-07-366190-2 |edition=2nd |series=McGraw-Hill series in forest resources |location=Boston}}</ref>

The more biodiverse the hardwood-forest ecosystem, the more challenges and opportunities its managers face. Managers aim for sustainable forest management to keep their cash crop renewing itself, using [[silvicultural]] practices that include growing, selling, controlling insects and most diseases, providing manure, applying herbicide treatments, and thinning.<ref name=":1" />

But management can also harm the ecosystem; for example, machinery used in a timber harvest can compact the soil, stress the root system, reduce tree growth, lengthen the time needed for a stand to mature to harvestability. Machinery can also damage the [[understory]], disturbing wildlife habitat and prevent regeneration.<ref name=":1" />
